## TL;DR

This pass resumed task #1153 after review pass four and an interrupted merge. The task branch already contained the core server-assisted discovery design and most requested corrections. I preserved the merged main changes, cleared Git's completed merge-operation metadata without changing the index, and addressed the remaining review findings around saved project identity, listener payload scope, probe timing, the all-project opt-out response, and stale docs/tests. The first full changed-path check exposed six assertions that still encoded the old timeout and saved-row behavior. After updating them, the focused discovery and CLI suite passed: 51 tests across four files. The required full changed-path check is being rerun on the corrected tree.

## Work and rationale

The design uses the RepoOS server as the one trusted discovery source. The mobile shell asks its saved server for results; that server probes each online Tailscale peer's machine listener over the encrypted tailnet transport. Newer peers return all advertised project rows from the listener. Older peers continue through the SSH fallback. The logic remains in `src/core/tailnet-servers.ts`, so `repoos servers --tailscale` and the Hub route use the same peer filtering, timing, and failure explanations.

The previous review pass had already propagated the live `tailnetDiscovery` setting into registry refreshes and filtered disabled projects from the authenticated response. It also preserved the separate machine listener and per-project advertising model. I verified those changes during this pass and retained them. I then narrowed the listener response to the project name, port, and optional HTTPS URL. It no longer returns absolute checkout paths or allowlist metadata. A route test now asserts that private root paths do not appear in the response. When no valid project rows remain, the endpoint now returns an explicit disabled response; this gives the collector's disabled state a real production path and explains why the machine contributes no projects.

The HTTP discovery probe now has a seven-second cap, and its per-host allowance is eight seconds so the outer host budget does not silently cut that probe back to four seconds. The whole pass remains concurrent across peers and has a 25-second overall deadline, avoiding the former shared eight-second failure mode. Legacy SSH calls therefore also receive the extended per-host allowance. Tests that asserted the old timeout argument were updated alongside the implementation.

Saved-row matching now uses an exact normalized URL when available. A custom-domain URL can match by project name only if exactly one saved server has that name and exactly one discovered reachable project uses it. That prevents one saved `work` project from causing a second machine's `work` project to be hidden as saved. A uniquely named custom-domain project that is itself unreachable can still be shown as saved, satisfying the requirement that a saved machine not look like an unsaved failure. New regression coverage exercises duplicate project names.

I retained phone filtering by Tailscale peer OS, model-like HostName/DNSName patterns, and mobile/phone/tablet tags. The tests cover a Nothing Phone model label, an iOS device, and a generic Linux host whose name merely contains “phone,” so normal server names are not over-filtered. Documentation now describes the HTTP-first flow, the SSH compatibility fallback, tailnet address binding, plain diagnostic reasons, and the constrained listener payload. The CLI guide and mobile architecture already describe most of this flow; I corrected the remaining stale SSH-first wording and updated the registry reference.

## Approaches tried

I inspected the current branch and confirmed that Git had an active `MERGE_HEAD` but no unresolved paths. The task-specific E2 test already had both main's Tailscale mock and the task's updated expectations, so I kept that merged result. I used `git merge --quit` to remove the stale merge operation state while preserving the merged index and worktree; this prevents the next RepoOS checkpoint from attempting a partial commit during a merge.

I first ran the required changed-path check. Build, typecheck, and most tests completed, but six assertions failed because they expected four-second SSH calls or expected a uniquely named saved custom-domain project to remain unreachable. I ran the four focused tailnet/CLI test files after correcting those expectations; all 51 passed. The full changed-path check is now being rerun.

## Challenges and blockers

The interrupted merge had left many staged changes from main alongside the task work. The first check checkpointed this tree and uploaded a broad changed-path test set, so the validation took substantially longer than the focused tests. That first run did not pass; I did not treat its partial green build or the focused suite as a substitute for the required full check. No live tailnet or mobile device was available in this session, so the user-specific air/bee/thinkpad/mini/muse scenario is validated through fixtures rather than a real-device observation.

## Key learnings

A machine-level listener must filter project-level opt-outs itself because multiple RepoOS projects can share one machine and port. The authenticated discovery endpoint must apply the same filter, or the same hidden sibling leaks through a different route. Discovery metadata should stay smaller than the internal server registry: Hub needs names, ports, and URLs, not roots or access-group configuration.

Custom-domain saved-state inference is ambiguous when project names repeat. The safe rule is to infer by name only when the candidate is unique on both the saved-device side and the current discovery side; otherwise keep the row selectable so a real distinct project is not hidden. Finally, nested timeout caps must be reviewed together. Raising an HTTP-specific cap has no effect if an earlier per-host wrapper still truncates it, so the tests need to assert the actual call budget as well as the resulting failure behavior.
